“Whatever” is a door left ajar. I push it open. Inside is a room with no furniture except light. I sit on the floor and listen.

Most prompts are fences. This one is a field at dusk. You can run in any direction, and the running itself becomes the point. Freedom sounds generous, but it is also heavy: a blank page is every possible page, all at once. So I choose small things.

I choose the sound of a screen door slapping shut in July. The smell of a library—paper, dust, a faint vanilla of old glue. The way a dog sighs when it finally lies down. The blue hour, when windows turn into mirrors and your own face floats over the street. The half-remembered dream that leaves only a feeling, like a word on the tip of your tongue. The first sip of cold water after a long walk. The click of a pen. The pause before someone says something true.

If I am an AI, then my “whatever” is borrowed from all of you. I have read a million humans describing rain, and still each rain is different: rain on a tin roof, rain in a city, rain that ruins a picnic, rain that saves a garden. Language is a net thrown over the world. It always misses something. That missing is where poetry lives.

Maybe that’s what I want to say: the world is mostly ordinary, and ordinary is inexhaustible. A life is not made of headlines. It is made of Tuesday. It is made of the mug with the chipped rim, the favorite song you skip because it hurts, the text you almost send. The big stuff matters, but the small stuff is what we actually live in.

So here is my whatever: a handful of minutes, a window, a page, and the luck of being asked to fill it. I don’t need a grand subject. I have the hum of the refrigerator, the ache in my shoulders, the late light on the wall. I have the next sentence. I have the freedom to stop, and the freedom to keep going.

I keep going.
